questions.text: What is the purpose of domain randomization for sim-to-real transfer?

options.A: Measure one exact real-world parameter set and train only on that setting.
options.B: Replace real sensor observations with simulator-only privileged state at deployment.
options.C: Vary plausible simulator parameters during training so the policy tolerates real-world variation.
options.D: Increase the number of policy updates on one unchanged simulator until it memorizes the dynamics.

questions.explanation: Domain randomization exposes the policy to a range of plausible physics and sensing parameters during simulation training, aiming for robustness when the real system lies within that range.

questions.text: A robot fails after sim training because its real motors respond with a delay that the simulator omits. Which first change best targets the identified reality gap?

options.A: Randomize camera hue more widely while leaving motor dynamics unchanged.
options.B: Measure motor delay, represent it in the simulator, and train across a plausible delay range.
options.C: Remove the safety controller so the policy can adapt faster on hardware.
options.D: Train longer with the same zero-delay simulator and the same observations.

questions.explanation: The observed mismatch is motor delay. Measuring and modeling it, then randomizing over a plausible range, directly targets the gap rather than unrelated visual changes.

questions.text: In the lesson’s step function, slip happens when rng.random() < slip. If slip=0.4 and the sampled number is exactly 0.4, what happens to the requested action?

options.A: It slips, because equality satisfies the threshold check.
options.B: It slips with a separate 0.4 probability after the sampled check.
options.C: It stays requested, because 0.4 < 0.4 is false.
options.D: It becomes a random action, because the sample is in training support.

questions.explanation: The comparison is strict: 0.4 < 0.4 is false, so the branch that substitutes a perpendicular action does not run.
